items.title: Rusty Dedrick interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998
items.q: he picked me and Don Elliott to be the players. And the rhythm section was known at that time as the NBC rhythm section... And we just went in and played.

ctx.x: How did your association with Don Elliott come about?

Well Riverside Records was a very well respected jazz label, like Keynote, and there were others that go way back. And I recorded for Keynote under my own name and they went bankrupt. Well Riverside didn’t go bankrupt. And Dick had a call to do something for them and it was his concept. And he said he’d like to do, that was that thing called “Counterpoint for Six Valves.” He’d like to do that and he wrote up some little duets and he picked me and Don Elliott to be the players. items.title: Rusty Dedrick interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998
items.q: His recordings include collaborations with Don Elliot

ctx.x: Lyle “Rusty” Dedrick was born in Delevan, New York on July 12, 1918. His family was engaged in farming but both he and his brother Art were attracted to the music business, taking up the trumpet and trombone. Starting in 1938, Rusty toured with Dick Stabile, Red Norvo and Claude Thornhill, eventually establishing himself in the active recording scene in New York City. He has arranged music for numerous ensembles and jazz artists and directed the Jazz Studies Department at the Manhattan School of Music in the…
Rusty was interviewed in Ellenville, New York on June 23, 1998, by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.
